cards.front: What four categories should you ask Claude to separate when structuring requirements from messy notes?
cards.back: **Requirements** (what it must do), **constraints** (limits), **assumptions** (believed but unconfirmed) and **open questions** (to ask a human).

cards.front: A request is vague ("improve onboarding"). What should you ask Claude to do before drafting?
cards.back: Ask you **clarifying questions** first (volume, owners, pain points, policy limits). Your answers become the context for the draft.

cards.front: Name six factors for scoring whether a task is a good Claude use case.
cards.back: Frequency, effort today, error impact, data sensitivity, verifiability (can a human check it quickly?), and whether it needs live systems.

cards.front: Which use cases should a team start with?
cards.back: **High-value, low-risk, repeatable** tasks that a human can review easily, such as meeting summaries, standard first drafts and feedback themes.

cards.front: Who confirms the final requirements: Claude or stakeholders?
cards.back: The **stakeholders**. Claude structures and challenges the thinking; it does not know your unwritten rules or internal history unless told.

cards.front: Four ways to use Claude as a critic of a requirements draft?
cards.back: Ask for edge cases, conflicting requirements, testable rewording, and objections from different stakeholder perspectives.

cards.front: When is Research the right feature?
cards.back: For a **multi-source investigation that needs citations**. Claude runs searches that build on each other and returns a cited report in minutes.

cards.front: Research prerequisites and costs (at the time of writing)?
cards.back: Paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise), **web search must be on**, and Research **uses usage limits faster** than ordinary chats.

cards.front: Can Research use internal content?
cards.back: Yes. It can draw on connected Google Workspace content (Gmail, Calendar, Docs) alongside web sources.

cards.front: Research gave you a cited report for executives. Next step?
cards.back: Open and **verify the key sources** (numbers, quotes, dates) and flag single-source claims. Citations are checkable, not proof.

cards.front: Two rules for Claude-drafted project plans?
cards.back: 1. Give Claude the **real constraints** (team, deadlines, budget, approvals). 2. Ask it to **list its assumptions**, and have a human validate the plan.

cards.front: Four steps to optimize a process with Claude?
cards.back: **Map** the current flow, **find friction** (waits, hand-offs, rework), **classify** each step (keep, remove, simplify, Claude-assist), **propose** a future state.

cards.front: Which process steps should stay with humans even after optimization?
cards.back: Approvals, commitments, and **decisions about people**. Automatic system-to-system data movement usually needs a technical build.

cards.front: What is an Artifact (Help Center definition, in short)?
cards.back: Significant, **self-contained** content (typically over 15 lines) you're likely to edit, reuse or share: documents, diagrams, dashboards, small interactive tools. Starts private; can be published and shared.

cards.front: Why prototype with Claude instead of describing the solution in words?
cards.back: People react to something concrete far better than to an abstract description, so feedback is faster and more specific.

cards.front: After user feedback on a prototype, regenerate from scratch or make targeted edits?
cards.back: **Targeted edits**: name exactly what to change and what to keep. Regenerating throws away what already works.

cards.front: Five signs a solution has crossed into Developer or Architect territory.
cards.back: Needs live data in company systems; a custom connector, MCP server or API integration; runs unattended or takes actions on its own; high-volume production reliability; sensitive data outside approved tools.

cards.front: What should you hand over when escalating a prototype?
cards.back: The prototype itself, the requirements, **real test examples including failures**, and user feedback. It is the clearest spec the builders can get.

cards.front: Which feature packages a reusable assistant for a recurring team task?
cards.back: A **Project** with instructions and knowledge files (self-contained workspace with its own chats and knowledge base).

cards.front: Augment vs redesign?
cards.back: **Augment**: Claude improves one step; the process and owners stay the same. **Redesign**: the process is rethought around what Claude makes cheap. It is riskier and needs buy-in.

cards.front: Which usually comes first, augment or redesign?
cards.back: **Augment first** to build evidence of reliability in your context, then redesign where the evidence supports it.

cards.front: Where must a human checkpoint sit in a Claude-assisted workflow?
cards.back: Wherever errors are costly: external, customer or regulator-facing output; legal, financial or medical content; **decisions about people**. Give each checkpoint a named owner.

cards.front: What is the rubber-stamp trap and how do you prevent it?
cards.back: Reviewers approve without reading once outputs look good. Prevent it with checklists, spot checks and tracking correction rates.

cards.front: Five things to measure before and after integrating Claude.
cards.back: Time per item, throughput, quality (errors, rework), consistency, and staff or customer satisfaction. You need a **baseline** first.

cards.front: Speed went up but error rate also went up. Is the integration done?
cards.back: No. Adjust the instructions, knowledge or checkpoint before scaling. Speed alone isn't success.

cards.front: Claude drafts a rejection letter. Who decides the application is rejected?
cards.back: A **person**. Augmenting judgment is not replacing it.

cards.front: How should you frame Claude's value for stakeholders?
cards.back: In **business outcomes** (time saved, capacity, consistency, quality, speed, coverage), backed by **pilot evidence**, not features or a single demo.

cards.front: Name five limitations to disclose honestly.
cards.back: Hallucinations, knowledge cutoff, no internal context unless provided, long-thread drift, run-to-run variation (plus data-handling rules and the fact that accountability stays human).

cards.front: Your pilot review caught three errors. Include them in the executive update?
cards.back: Yes. Reporting caught errors with the fix shows the controls work and builds credibility. Hiding them is a trap.

cards.front: What do executives want in an update?
cards.back: Outcome, evidence, risk, cost of the next step and the **decision you need**, ideally on one page.

cards.front: A stakeholder asks for Claude to "just connect to our CRM and act automatically". Your reply?
cards.back: Explain it needs a **Developer or Architect** build (integration or agent), not a bigger prompt. Offer your prototype and requirements as the starting point.

cards.front: Three phrases that signal overpromising.
cards.back: "Fully automated", "eliminates errors", "no review needed".

cards.front: What are the four outcomes at the end of a pilot?
cards.back: **Scale**, **adjust and re-run**, **escalate** to technical roles, or **stop**. Stopping is a valid result.

cards.front: Most important pilot quality metric?
cards.back: **Errors that escaped review**. It shows whether the human checkpoint actually works.

cards.front: What are the four Ds of Anthropic's AI Fluency framework?
cards.back: **Delegation** (what humans vs AI do), **Description** (communicating with AI), **Discernment** (evaluating output), **Diligence** (responsible, safe use).

cards.front: How do connectors fit into workflow integration for an Associate?
cards.back: They let Claude read context from approved tools (for example Google Drive, Gmail, Calendar). Use the ones your plan and admins enable; don't bolt on unapproved tools.
